lessons.title: Settings that cut your screen time (and stress)

steps.title: Setting up focus mode
steps.body: With a focus mode (like 'Studying' or 'Sleep') you decide which notifications come through at certain times and which don't. Set this up under Settings > Focus — handy during an exam, or when you finally want to sleep without every like lighting up your screen.

steps.title: Cleaning up notifications
steps.body: Go to Settings > Notifications and turn off what you don't need, per app. Cuts a lot of distraction and doomscrolling, without missing important messages.

steps.title: Checking screen time (no guilt required)
steps.body: Your phone tracks (Settings > Screen Time / Digital Wellbeing) how much time you spend in which app. No judgment needed — just useful to see whether it matches how you actually want to spend your time.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Set up a focus mode and limit notifications from at least two apps that distract you.

steps.title: Automations (routines)
steps.body: With Google Assistant routines or iPhone 'Shortcuts', for example, you can have something happen automatically, like: reading out the weather and your first appointment automatically every morning.

steps.title: Managing storage smartly
steps.body: Have photos and videos automatically go to the cloud (as covered in module 6) and then delete them from your phone itself, to free up space without losing anything — handy when your phone says 'storage full' right when you need to save something important.

steps.title: Grouping apps into folders
steps.body: Drag one app icon onto another to create a folder. This keeps your home screen tidy — and stops you from accidentally tapping a distracting app instead of the one you meant to open.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Create a folder on your home screen and group a few similar apps into it.

lessons.title: AI on your phone for everyday tasks

steps.title: More than a voice assistant
steps.body: The Gemini app (Google) or ChatGPT app can hold real conversations, write text, and think things through with you — useful for much more than just 'set an alarm'.

steps.title: Having a photo explained or translated
steps.body: Take a photo of, say, a menu in another language while traveling, or a confusing college form, and ask the AI app to translate or explain it — via the camera feature built into the app.

steps.title: Quickly drafting a message
steps.body: Need to send an email to a teacher or employer quickly but not sure how to start? Briefly describe the situation to the AI and ask for a draft, which you then adjust and put in your own style.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Ask Gemini to write a short message for a situation from your own life, then adjust it to your own style.

lessons.title: The limits of AI on your phone

steps.title: What AI assistants aren't good at
steps.body: An AI app can sound convincing even when the answer is factually wrong. Never blindly trust important information (medical, financial, legal, or for school) — check it with a reliable source.

steps.title: Privacy of voice commands
steps.body: Voice commands are often (partly) processed via the company's servers. Never say sensitive information like passwords or PINs out loud to a voice assistant, especially not in public.

steps.title: When you need to think for yourself
steps.body: Use AI on your phone as quick help or a first draft, but make the final decision yourself on anything that matters — an AI app is no substitute for your own judgment.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Think of a situation where you would use an AI app on your phone, and one where you would deliberately choose not to.
